passage: In the Class 10 physics lab, Vidya ma'am was explaining why both bulbs in a parallel circuit stayed bright. Raghav leaned back on his stool. "Ma'am, that's not fully right," he said. "I watched a series on electricity. Current is basically like water, so the second bulb should be dimmer." A few students turned. Vidya ma'am handed him the wires. "Show us." Raghav connected them confidently, flipped the switch, and both bulbs glowed equally bright. He stared. "Maybe the battery's wrong." "Try another." Same result. "The videos were really detailed," he muttered, pulling at his sleeve. Ma'am smiled. "Water is a helpful picture. It just has limits you haven't met yet."

passage:
Science teacher's note, Class 9

Tarun has become very interested in black holes, which is wonderful. Over the holidays he watched several videos about them.

In class today, when I explained that nothing, not even light, escapes from inside a black hole, he stood up and said, "That's outdated, ma'am, I saw a video that proves light comes out." He said it with complete certainty and told the class he probably knew more about black holes than I did.

I didn't mock him. I asked him to explain to the class what an event horizon is. He started confidently, then got tangled. He couldn't say what the video had actually claimed. He sat down quietly.

After class, I gave him a short article that explains Hawking radiation properly, and asked him to present it next week. His ideas were half-right; he just couldn't tell which half yet.

Leela

qa.a: I saw a video that proves light comes out.

qa.q: Why did Tarun feel so sure he knew more than the teacher?
qa.a: Tarun felt confident and excited after watching several videos, and didn't yet know enough to see what he was missing.

qa.q: What did Leela do that helped Tarun see the gaps?
qa.a: Leela asked Tarun to explain an event horizon himself, so the gaps showed, then gave him a proper article to present.

qa.q: How might Tarun's classmates have felt when he said he knew more than the teacher?
qa.a: Some classmates may have felt impressed, others uncomfortable or amused, and many probably watched to see how the teacher would react.

passage:
Thursday night

Today in history class I told Mr Bhatia he was wrong about the Mughal empire. I've watched like six videos on it this month and one guy explained that everything we learn in textbooks is wrong.

I said it loud. The whole class turned around. Mr Bhatia didn't get angry. He asked me to name three sources the video used.

I couldn't. I said, "He just knows, he has a million subscribers."

Mr Bhatia asked what I knew about the Mansabdari system. I had literally never heard of it.

Vikas whispered, "Bro, you got owned." I wanted to disappear.

But now I'm thinking. The video felt so complete. I thought I understood everything. But I didn't even know what I didn't know.

Mr Bhatia said I can borrow his book on the Mughals. Maybe I will. Quietly.

Amandeep

qa.a: Like six videos on it this month.
